summary: John gave evidence on alleged unlawful killings by SAPS task teams in KwaZulu-Natal and on alleged collusion between officers and tow-truck operators linked to drug trafficking and turf disputes. He told the commission that 149 people had died in 77 incidents involving task team operations between April 2023 and May 2026. He described a pattern in which operations took place late at night, officers covered their faces, and all suspects present were killed, and said the firearms recovered were often inconsistent with the cash-in-transit robbery profile attributed to those killed. He alleged that some officers received payments from tow-truck operators and drug gang figures for protection and for targeted killings, and connected the April 2023 killing of Bevan Loftus to an alleged offer of R2.5-million to Lieutenant-Colonel Deena Govender by a rival operator. Evidence was also heard about R2.3-million allegedly deposited into the accounts of a police officer and his wife.

summary: Day 34 dealt with the handover of the 121 (later found to be 123) dockets between the KZN Political Killings Task Team (PKTT) and SAPS head office in Pretoria. summary: On Day 29, retired Ekurhuleni Metro Police Department (EMPD) Deputy Chief Commissioner Revo Spies continued his testimony, led by evidence leader Adv Sello SC, detailing his 2023 internal investigation into Brigadier Julius (JD) Mkhwanazi's dealings with CAT VIP Protection and Medicare 24/Anubis Protection Services, including memoranda of understanding that Spies said purported to grant the private firms law-enforcement functions such as vehicle registration, blue-light use, medical/legal assistance and crime-scene response. He closed the day describing 2023 death threats against him after a State Security Agency assessment found colleagues had discussed hiring a hitman, and said the city manager declined to fund protective measures. summary: The Commission continued its inquiry into alleged Hawks (DPCI) interference in the 6 December 2024 SAPS takedown at Katiso Molefe's Sandton home, hearing the second batch of three witness statements (Sections 4-6 of the bundle). Gauteng Traffic Police's George Raftopoulos ("Chief George") described dispatching a helicopter at a colleague's request and denied any interference. DPCI Warrant Officer Sabelo Nkosi described being diverted from a North West operation to an "insignificant verification" in Sandton on Brigadier Mokoena's instruction, and confirmed police vehicles at the scene well before Captain Kruger did. summary: Day 20 (27 October 2025) was devoted entirely to testimony from Brigadier Mishak Mkhabela, SAPS's national Head of the Ballistics Section, who explained how ballistics comparison and the IBIS/ABIS automated matching system work and detailed severe capacity constraints (roughly 29,000 crime-linked firearms held in storage nationally, over 41,000 ballistics cases and 108,000 IBIS entries awaiting work, and an understaffed KwaZulu-Natal IBIS unit). Extensive evidence then traced the ballistics audit trail for the 17 April 2024 murder of Armand Swart in Vereeniging and the same-day Bramley arrest of suspects found with an AK-47, a Taurus pistol, a CZ pistol and other firearms, including cross-referencing errors in the investigating analyst's original affidavit and a previously undisclosed third version of that affidavit. ABIS matching, only completed roughly a year after the seizure, linked the Bramley firearms to more than two dozen other serious crimes nationally, including cases the Commission permitted naming: the attempted murder of Tebogo Thobejane, and the murders of DJ Sumbody, DJ Vintos and Don Tindleni. The evidence leader proposed an independent re-examination of the ballistics evidence given the unexplained affidavit discrepancies, a decision left pending a scheduled 31 October meeting between SAPS ballistics and the prosecutor.

summary: The Commission resumed with argument by Adv Sello SC clarifying and amending the in-camera ruling made on Day 13, so that Witnesses A, B and C could testify remotely, in public, with their voices unaltered but their images not broadcast and their names withheld for the time being; the Chairperson granted the amendment. Witness A, a SAPS Organised Crime investigator, then gave evidence led by Adv Segeels-Ncube SC concerning the investigation into the April 2024 murder of Armand Swart in Vereeniging, describing four related crime scenes (Bramley/Q, the Vereeniging Q-Tech office park, and the Klip River R59 Engen garage), the arrest of Warrant Officer Michael Pule Tau, Musa Kekana and Tiego Floyd Mabusela, and physical, cellphone and CCTV evidence linking the accused to Katiso Molefe in the period before and after the murder. Witness A testified to being followed and intimidated by fellow police officers after Tau's first court appearance, to a meeting with Major-General (referred to as General) Shibiri in which Shibiri referenced "three envelopes" allegedly available to secure bail for Tau, and to two subsequent social gatherings hosted by one Vusi Ndlala at which Shibiri and other senior officers were present. He further testified to apparent tampering or omission in an initial ballistics report prepared by Warrant Officer Makgotloe that failed to address 15 cartridges recovered from the Viano, to Tau's release on bail on 2 August 2024 (which Ndlala appeared to have predicted), to an unsuccessful attempt by two officers from the Cold Case Unit to obtain the docket, and to the eventual provision of protection and a Threat and Risk Assessment classifying the investigating team as high risk. Commissioners repeatedly sought clarification of timelines, vehicle identifications, and the evidentiary basis for inferences drawn in the witness statement, and corrected several transcription and paragraph-reference errors on the record.

He first addressed the constitutional and policy framework governing the Minister of Police's relationship with the National Commissioner under sections 205, 206 and 207(2), maintaining that operational and managerial matters fall exclusively within his own remit and that he would refuse to comply with an instruction from the Minister that strayed into that area. He then gave a detailed history of the Political Killings Task Team (PKTT): its 2018 establishment following IMC direction under President Ramaphosa, its command structure, funding and extension processes, its expansion to the University of Fort Hare murders and to killings of traditional leaders, and statistics on dockets, arrests and convictions, which he characterised as showing an "unmatched success rate," a characterisation the Chairperson and Commissioners probed closely against the raw docket-finalisation figures. Masemola described the Gauteng Counter Intelligence Operation, the secondment of PKTT members to Gauteng, and the resulting arrests of Mr Katiso Molefe and Mr Vusumuzi "Cat" Matlala. He then testified at length about the Minister's 31 December 2024 letter directing immediate disbandment of the PKTT, his own view that the instruction was unlawful as an encroachment on operational matters, his instruction to Lt-Gen Sibiya to prepare a phased wind-down plan rather than immediate disbandment, and Lt-Gen Sibiya's subsequent issuing of his own disbandment letter under his own name on 17 January 2025 in what Masemola characterised as defiance of his instruction. He also described briefing the Minister on 16 January 2025 on an implicated "Big Five" syndicate, in which Lt-Gen Sibiya, Mr Molefe and Mr Matlala were named, while separately confirming that the internal investigation into Sibiya's alleged associations remained unsubstantiated and under investigation. The Chairperson repeatedly and pointedly challenged Masemola on the apparent inconsistency between his stated position that he would never obey an unlawful instruction and his subsequent acceptance, in a modified "phased" form, of the disbandment; Masemola ultimately agreed he had "relented" in substance while insisting the team had, as of the hearing, never actually been disbanded.

summary: On Day 3 (19 September 2025) Lieutenant General Nhlanhla Mkhwanazi, KwaZulu-Natal Provincial Commissioner, continued his sworn testimony, completing his evidence on Mr Brown Mogotsi (an associate of Minister of Police Senzo Mchunu) and turning to alleged political interference by the Executive, the Judiciary and the National Commissioner's office. He testified about WhatsApp communications with Mogotsi (Annexure MK17) that he said showed Mogotsi had access to a Crime Intelligence presentation, advance knowledge of the Minister's letter disbanding the Political Killings Task Team (PKTT), and contact with Vusimuzi "Cat" Matlala. He described his 2021-2022 deployment of KZN detectives to Richards Bay Minerals and the subsequent redeployment as a "GCI Ops" under Deputy National Commissioner Lt Gen Sibiya, and gave an account of the 5 February 2025 Councillor murder in iLembe district in which he said the Minister pressured District Commissioner Maj Gen Gopaul about the case being assigned to the PKTT. He also testified about Major General Sibiya's employment history, including an unsigned City of Johannesburg letter (MK23) that flagged alleged irregularities before Sibiya joined SAPS, and about historical interference he said he experienced regarding Lt Gen Richard Mdluli in 2011-2012 (detailed in his Zondo Commission affidavit, MK22). He described what he characterised as retaliatory action against himself and Task Team members, including arrests by IDAC and bail conditions barring Crime Intelligence members from Crime Intelligence premises, and the NPA's declining to prosecute Ms Nellie Ndlovu over drugs and ammunition found at Qalakabusha correctional facility (MK26). The Chairperson repeatedly sought clarification on dates, the scope of instructions to disband the PKTT, and the reliability of the witness's inferences from WhatsApp messages, and the evidence leaders flagged unresolved documentation issues, including a missing page of MK17 and an unsigned affidavit from Gopaul.

rulings.description: NPA (Adv Mkhonza) declined to prosecute Ms Nellie Joyce Ndlovu for unlawful possession of ammunition and drugs, finding no prospect of successful prosecution since the items were found outside her house in a dustbin accessible to others.

A Magistrate imposed a bail condition barring arrested Crime Intelligence members from entering any Crime Intelligence premises in South Africa; a different Magistrate later released one co-accused on bail without that restriction, ruling it was not the Court's role to set such conditions.

summary: Day 1 of the Madlanga Commission opened with the Chairperson's introductory remarks and an opening address by Chief Evidence Leader Adv Terry Motau SC, who outlined the Commission's mandate, its three-phase approach, and a timeline of material events from July 2018 to July 2025. The Commission then heard sworn testimony from its first witness, Lt Gen Nhlanhla Sibusiso Mkhwanazi, Provincial Commissioner of Police in KwaZulu-Natal, led by Adv Mahlape Sello SC. Mkhwanazi gave his professional background, outlined the SAPS constitutional and legislative structure, and testified in detail about the establishment, funding, mandate and successes of the KwaZulu-Natal Political Killings Task Team (PKTT), including its expansion to the Eastern Cape (University of Fort Hare cases) and to traditional-leader killings. He testified about the involvement of ten seconded PKTT members in the Gauteng Counter Intelligence Operations (GCI Ops) following threats to investigators on the Armand Swart murder case, reading into the record a letter from prosecutor Ms Coetzee describing those threats and syndicate links. He testified about Minister Mchunu's 31 December 2024 letter disbanding the PKTT, his unsuccessful efforts to raise the issue with the National Commissioner, the Minister, and the Portfolio Committee, and the subsequent transfer of 121 case dockets to Pretoria under Lt Gen Sibiya's direction without, he says, National Commissioner authorisation. The Chairperson pressed the witness on whether disbanding the PKTT was a policy matter (within the Minister's remit) or an operational matter, and Mkhwanazi maintained it was operational and therefore outside the Minister's constitutional authority. The day closed with the docket-transfer and eventual return of the dockets to KZN still under examination, to continue the next sitting day.
